title: Medical Negligence Claims: Why a Missing Case Sheet Can Decide the Case Against the Hospital
meta_description: What a hospital's failure to produce its complete case sheet does to its defence in a negligence complaint, illustrated by a Rs 99 lakh Kakinada order.
intro: Medical negligence complaints in India start from a demanding position for the complainant: the burden of proving negligence and a deficiency in service lies squarely on the patient or family bringing the complaint, and consumer commissions have repeatedly said that negligence has to be established, not presumed. A hospital that is confident its treatment decisions were sound often assumes this burden alone will carry the day. A 2026 Kakinada District Consumer Commission order is a useful corrective, showing how a hospital's own failure to produce the complete case sheet and treatment records can tip a case decisively, even where the complainant's own expert evidence is thin.
This guide looks at what the case sheet actually proves in a negligence dispute, what the Kakinada order did with a records gap, and what both complainants and hospitals should take from it.

sections.heading: Why the Burden Normally Sits With the Complainant
paragraphs: The settled position, reflected in rulings such as the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission's treatment of Calcutta Medical Research Institute v. Bimalesh Chatterjee and Kanhaiya Kumar Singh v. Park Medicare & Research Centre, is that medical negligence cannot be presumed from a bad outcome alone. The complainant has to show, through evidence, that the treatment fell short of the standard a reasonably competent professional would have provided in the same circumstances, and commentary on this line of cases notes that courts apply a higher evidentiary standard before holding a doctor liable than they might in an ordinary deficiency-of-service complaint against another kind of service provider.

This standard exists for good reason: medicine involves judgment calls under uncertainty, and a bad outcome does not automatically mean a wrong decision was made at the time. But the standard assumes the complainant has some realistic way to test whether the treatment decisions were sound, and that realistic path runs almost entirely through the hospital's own records, since the complainant and family were rarely in a position to observe or document the clinical reasoning as it happened.

sections.heading: What the Kakinada Order Actually Found
paragraphs: The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission in Kakinada directed Medicover Hospitals, Nellore, and its treating cardiologist to pay Rs 99 lakh in compensation, plus costs, over the death of a patient who had been admitted on 28 February 2025 with a serious cardiac condition and died on 2 March 2025, days after being administered dialysis. The commission found the hospital could not justify the decision to administer dialysis to a patient with the cardiac complications on record, and, critically, that the hospital failed to produce the complete medical case sheet and other contemporaneous treatment records that might have explained or supported that clinical decision.

The order's structure matters as much as its outcome. The commission did not treat the missing records as a side issue to note in passing while deciding the case on other evidence. It treated the gap in the records as itself supporting the negligence finding, alongside the substantive clinical question of whether dialysis was appropriate given the patient's cardiac history. Half the awarded amount was directed to be held for the patient's minor daughter in a fixed deposit until she comes of age, with compliance required within 45 days of the order.

sections.heading: Why an Incomplete Record Gets Treated as Evidence Against the Hospital
paragraphs: The logic here is not simply that missing records are suspicious, though that intuition is not wrong either. It reflects a structural point about who actually controls the evidence in a medical negligence dispute. The hospital creates and keeps the case sheet, decides what gets documented contemporaneously, and is the only party capable of producing a complete record of what was actually done and why. When that same party cannot produce a complete record, or cannot point to anything in the records it does produce that justifies a specific clinical decision under challenge, treating the gap as supporting an adverse inference is a reasonable response to an evidentiary asymmetry the hospital itself created.

This differs from, but interacts closely with, the general rule that the complainant carries the initial burden. One line of appellate commentary notes that once a complainant has discharged that initial burden by making out a prima facie case of negligence, the onus can shift to the hospital or doctor to show there was no lack of care. A significant, unexplained gap in the hospital's own contemporaneous records is exactly the kind of fact that can tip a borderline case from 'complainant has not yet shown enough' into 'the hospital has not met what is now its burden to explain', without requiring the kind of dramatic, self-evident error that res ipsa loquitur cases, such as a surgical instrument left inside a patient, typically involve.

sections.heading: What a Hospital Should Take From This
paragraphs: Maintaining a complete, contemporaneous case sheet is not just good clinical practice or a hygiene factor for internal audits. It is a central legal defence, and the Kakinada order shows exactly how a gap discovered only during litigation becomes very difficult to explain away after the fact. A treating team that made a defensible, if debatable, clinical call under real time pressure is in a far stronger position if that reasoning was documented as it happened than if it has to be reconstructed, months or years later, through recollection and argument once a complaint has been filed.

For hospital administrators and risk management teams, the practical takeaway is to treat case sheet completeness, including documented reasoning for any treatment decision that departs from an obvious or routine course, especially where a patient's recorded history includes a condition that might contraindicate a planned intervention, as a standing compliance priority rather than something reviewed only after an adverse outcome has already occurred.

sections.heading: What a Complainant Should Do Early in the Dispute
paragraphs: For a patient's family considering a negligence complaint, the practical lesson cuts the other way: request the complete treatment record and case sheet formally, in writing, as early as possible, ideally before filing the complaint itself. This serves two purposes at once. It gives the family's own medical expert something concrete to review before the complaint is drafted, which strengthens the substantive case, and it tests, in real time, whether the hospital can actually produce what it was obligated to maintain in the first place.

A hospital that responds promptly with a complete, well-organised record at least narrows the dispute to the substantive clinical question. A hospital that delays, produces an incomplete set, or cannot explain gaps when asked directly gives the complainant exactly the kind of evidentiary opening the Kakinada commission relied on. Either way, making this request early, and keeping a clear record of the request and the response, puts the complainant in a materially better position than waiting for the records to surface, if they do, only once the formal proceeding is already underway.

faqs.q: Who has the burden of proving medical negligence in a consumer complaint?
faqs.a: The complainant, as a general rule. Consumer commissions have consistently held that negligence must be established through evidence and cannot be presumed from a bad outcome alone, applying a higher evidentiary standard than in an ordinary deficiency-of-service complaint against a non-medical service provider.

faqs.q: What happened in the Kakinada case sheet ruling?
faqs.a: The Kakinada District Consumer Commission directed a Nellore hospital and its cardiologist to pay Rs 99 lakh after finding they could not justify administering dialysis to a patient with cardiac complications and failed to produce the complete case sheet and contemporaneous treatment records.

faqs.q: Can a missing medical record alone decide a negligence case?
faqs.a: It can weigh heavily, particularly where the hospital also cannot otherwise justify the specific clinical decision under challenge from whatever records it does produce. The Kakinada commission treated the records gap as supporting the negligence finding itself, not merely as a procedural shortcoming on the side.

faqs.q: Does the burden of proof ever shift to the hospital?
faqs.a: Once a complainant has made out a prima facie case of negligence, the practical weight can shift to the hospital or doctor to show there was no lack of care. A significant, unexplained gap in the hospital's own contemporaneous records can be the fact that tips a borderline case in the complainant's favour at that stage.

faqs.q: Should I request medical records before filing a negligence complaint?
faqs.a: Yes. Requesting the complete case sheet and treatment record in writing, before filing, both supports your expert's review of the substantive clinical question and tests whether the hospital can actually produce what it was required to maintain, which becomes important evidence either way.

references: Kakinada District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission order, CC No. 169 of 2025 (2026)
Calcutta Medical Research Institute v. Bimalesh Chatterjee (NCDRC)
Kanhaiya Kumar Singh v. Park Medicare & Research Centre (NCDRC)
verification_notes: Kakinada order facts (Medicover Hospitals, Nellore, and Dr. Paluru Manohar Reddy directed to pay Rs 99 lakh plus Rs 10,000 costs, patient admitted 28 February 2025 and died 2 March 2025, failure to justify dialysis and failure to produce the complete case sheet, 45-day compliance period, Rs 50 lakh apportioned to the minor daughter in fixed deposit) confirmed across Medical Dialogues and LiveLaw reporting; the order's own stated date showed a discrepancy between the commission's records (30.06.2026) and the signed order text (30 July 2026), so this guide does not state a specific decision date and relies instead on the confirmed August 2026 media reporting window. General burden-of-proof rule (complainant bears initial burden, negligence not presumed) and the shifting-burden principle confirmed via Nishith Desai's summary citing Calcutta Medical Research Institute and Kanhaiya Kumar Singh; the Nishith Desai source itself was the only one located for the shifting-burden principle, so it is presented as appellate commentary rather than a directly quoted Supreme Court holding, consistent with the search results available. No claim is made that the Kakinada order is binding precedent beyond its own district-level standing.
